reviewedCourses.name: Personal & Professional Development
reviewedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.

reviewedCourses.name: Native American Histories
reviewedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies Native American social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present through Indigenous perspectives and collaborative inquiry. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to contemporary resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, relational accountability and reciprocity inform work with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders. Arts-based collaborations and a public-history project develop respectful, accessible accounts of historical and contemporary issues.
reviewedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: This course introduces students to Native American history and life from the 19th through the 21st century.  It argues that power, fear, misogyny, education, genocide, and resilience shape the Indigenous past and present. Topics we explore include the “Stolen Lives” of Indian children forcibly taken from their homes and placed in Indian Boarding Schools from the 1830’s through the 1990’s; Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women and Girls in the twenty-first century; and the individual and community forms of cultural resistance and environmental regeneration that connect past with present and future generations. We learn from the Native American scholars and 2Spirit youth that speak to and with the class. Exchange of cultural and intellectual knowledge also happens when we work with Lakota students to address contemporary challenges. Legislation, memoir, novels, and Indigenous children’s stories are central to our studies. So are the analyses of contemporary music and artistic expressions and exhibitions, as well as Hollywood and Indigenous film featuring Native American histories and lives.

reviewedCourses.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
reviewedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies Athenian democracy through history, archaeology, literature, art and religion, including its exclusions and moments of crisis. Students analyze citizenship, social divisions, myth, ritual and cultural expression through primary texts and material evidence. A historically grounded assembly simulation explores political decision-making. Research reports connect ancient democracy to the present, while a collective cultural project for Middelburg experiments with participatory democratic collaboration.
reviewedCourses.officialDescriptionRead:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century._x000D_
Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants._x000D_
This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.

candidateAssessments.concept: Belief, theology, religious traditions and worldviews
candidateAssessments.assessment: UCR offers real study of philosophical questions about God and meaning, comparative myths, religious art and material culture, and ethics. A strengthened combination of these courses still does not sustain inquiry into theological sources, Christian faith and its interpretation, lived religious practice and the relationship between religious tradition and contemporary church and society that defines this bachelor. General cultural interpretation and public ethics provide relevant connections but do not together establish a defensible Theology programme.

Ethical theory, human rights, constitutional law, social justice and environmental movements are real substantive inquiry. Secular public responsibility does not implement theological ethical interpretation merely because the target asks justice/tolerance questions. It cannot bypass failure of a defensible closest response.

The actual minor combines general pedagogy/didactics6, subject didactics6, school placement/intervision15 and education research3. Rhetoric in Action provides real primary-school public speaking and youth resilience provides educational prevention, but neither establishes religion/worldview didactics or a sustained education-and-religion programme. Qualification absence alone is not the reason.

Actual minor includes sin/grace, religion/humanism/AI, God/evil, contemporary ethics, churches/interreligious dialogue and canon law. Philosophical God/agency and AI ethics give genuine connections, without establishing the religious and theological inquiry. Not rejected only for lack of a canonical credential.
